name: Uma Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Nothing you say will be linked to your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the hen house by six. We've got twelve thousand free-range laying hens in three sheds at Brook End, plus a bit of grassland and a few beef calves my husband Tom looks after on the side. The eggs roll down a belt into the packing room, and I check them, grade them and box them for the packer who collects on Tuesdays and Fridays. What I like is that it's steady, hens lay every day. What wears me out is the fear of bird flu, every winter, because one case nearby and we're all shut in.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use computers much for the work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: As little as I can. The packer sends orders by email, and Tom reads them, I don't. I've never used one of those AI chat things and I don't plan to. I've got a notebook for the flock, egg counts and feed, and it hasn't let me down in fifteen years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say not much, I suppose. Good for people who like that sort of thing. I'd talk about the egg price and the cost of feed, because that's what's actually going up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing to me. Hens don't read emails. I'd carry on with the notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as every year. Repaint the sheds in spring, renew the fox fencing, about two thousand, and keep a bit put by in case of bird flu. I'd leave the computer to Tom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Nothing to feel about, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the packer said the order system was changing to an AI one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tom to sort it, and I'd ring the driver, Gary, to check the numbers like I always do. As long as the right number of boxes leaves the yard, I don't care how they take the order. If they got it wrong, I'd want a person to shout at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep a bit put by for bird flu. How much is enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About four months of bills, which is roughly what we've got. When we were shut in for twelve weeks three winters ago, the hens kept laying but the free-range price dropped because they weren't outside. We ate into savings and I swore I'd never be caught short again.

S0.say: Not much, I suppose; it's good for people who like that sort of thing. What actually matters is the egg price and the cost of feed.
S0.think: It means nothing to me, because hens don't read emails. I'd carry on with my notebook for the flock, like I have for fifteen years.
S0.do: Repaints the sheds and renews the fox fencing for about two thousand, as usual. Keeps around four months of bills put by for bird flu and leaves anything on the computer to her husband Tom.
S0.feel: Fine, with nothing much to feel about.
S0.quote: I don't care how they take the order. If they got it wrong, I'd want a person to shout at.
S0.fieldNote: She is short, dry and entirely unbothered, and all her real worry goes to bird flu. Her rule is simple: a person she can phone when things go wrong. The twelve-week lockdown three winters ago shaped how she thinks about savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it'll sort itself out over ten years, it always does. I'd probably say young people should learn a trade. Not much more, I'm not one for opinions online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, slow is the only kind of change I can manage. But the bit about fewer beginners, our Freya is sixteen and wants to work in an office, in town, at the council or a bank. If they're hiring fewer, she'll be stuck at home with the hens, and she'd hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Freya to get a part-time job now, Saturdays at the garden centre, so she's got something on her record. I'd keep the farm the same. Maybe Tom would put the flock records on the computer, but I'd keep my notebook as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for the farm, worried for Freya. A small knot, not a big one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Freya couldn't find work, would you want her on the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, and I'd never say that to her face. Twelve thousand hens don't pay two wages, and she's not cut out for it, she gags at the muck. I'd rather she went to college and found something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any task you'd be glad to see disappear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grading. Holding eggs up to the light for cracks, eight hours, it does your eyes in. If a machine did that, and did it right, I'd not miss it. But I'd want to see it work for a year somewhere else first.

S1.say: It'll sort itself out over ten years, it always does. Young people should learn a trade, and I'm not one for opinions online.
S1.think: Slow change is the only kind I can manage. But my daughter Freya wants an office job in town, and if they hire fewer beginners she'll be stuck at home with the hens.
S1.do: Tells Freya to get a Saturday job at the garden centre now, so she has something on her record. Keeps the farm the same, and keeps her notebook even if Tom moves the records onto the computer.
S1.feel: Calm about the farm, with a small knot of worry for her daughter.
S1.quote: Twelve thousand hens don't pay two wages, and she's not cut out for it, she gags at the muck.
S1.fieldNote: She admitted privately that she doesn't want her daughter on the farm, which she'd never say to her. She'd accept a grading machine but only after seeing it work for a year elsewhere. Her views on the wider economy stay vague and unworried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's two sides to it. Some people will lose out and some will do well, and the politicians should stop shouting and agree something sensible. I wouldn't go to any rallies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the packer's office would be the first to go automatic, I'd bet on it. If I lose Gary on the phone and get a computer instead, that's the bit of the job I'd hate. I'm not sure it would change the money much, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make Tom learn whatever new ordering system they bring in, because I won't. I'd ring Gary while he's still there and ask him what's happening. And I'd keep the four months of savings exactly where they are and not touch them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when the weather changes and you can't say how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss about Gary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's been collecting our eggs for nine years. He knows when the hens are off lay, he knows Tom's mum died last spring, he asks after Freya. A computer can't do that, and it can't tell you the packer's cutting the price before it's in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it wouldn't change the money much. Are you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not sure. If the packer gets cheaper to run, they might pay a bit more, or they might just keep it. I'd guess keep it. Nobody's ever passed a saving down to the farm in my lifetime.

S2.say: There are two sides to it, and the politicians should stop shouting and agree something sensible. I wouldn't go to any rallies.
S2.think: The packer's office would be first to go automatic, and losing Gary on the phone is the part I'd hate. I'm not sure it would change the money much.
S2.do: Makes Tom learn any new ordering system and rings the driver Gary to ask what's happening while he's still there. Leaves the four months of savings untouched.
S2.feel: Uneasy, like a change in the weather she can't quite name.
S2.quote: Nobody's ever passed a saving down to the farm in my lifetime.
S2.fieldNote: Her worry is about losing a person, the egg driver of nine years, more than money. When I asked if she was sure about the money, she admitted she wasn't and turned quietly cynical. She hands every technology job to her husband.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a mess and both sides are to blame. The companies shouldn't keep it all, but the government shouldn't go mad with taxes either. Something in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, eggs are cheap food, and when people lose their jobs they eat more eggs, not fewer. So the farm might do all right. What I'd worry about is the free-range premium, that's the extra people pay for hens that go outside, because people who are short of money buy the cheap caged ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to the packer about a fixed price for a year, so I know where I stand. I'd hold off on any new shed, though we'd talked about one. And I'd tell Tom not to listen to his brother about buying shares, because when everyone says something's booming, that's when you keep your money in your pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not scared. More watchful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your house would be worth more. Would that change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It's not ours to sell, it's the farm, it's where the hens are. My sister in town would be pleased about her flat, I suppose. Good for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom's brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Neil, you bought a boat on credit in 2019 and sold it at a loss, don't tell us about booms. He'd laugh. He always laughs, that's his problem.

S3.say: It's a mess, and both sides are to blame. The companies shouldn't keep it all, but the government shouldn't go mad with taxes either.
S3.think: When people lose jobs they eat more eggs, so the farm might do all right. The risk is losing the free-range premium as people switch to cheap caged eggs.
S3.do: Asks the packer for a fixed price for a year and holds off on the new shed they'd discussed. Tells Tom not to follow his brother into buying shares during the boom.
S3.feel: Uneasy but not scared, more watchful than worried.
S3.quote: When everyone says something's booming, that's when you keep your money in your pocket.
S3.fieldNote: She worked out that cheap food like eggs might actually sell better in hard times, which was a sharp point. Her politics stay firmly in the middle, blaming both sides. Her caution with money showed in a funny jab at her brother-in-law's boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a step too far, they should go slower and look after people. I'd probably say it at the farmers' meeting, which is more than I usually say. I'd not go online about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one bothers me. Big egg farms with robots that clean the sheds, check the birds and pack the eggs would make them cheaper than I ever could. I'm not buying a robot, I wouldn't trust it with live birds, so I'd be the one left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the packer straight whether they'd keep buying from small free-range farms. If they said no, I'd look at selling eggs at the farm gate and to a couple of village shops, which pays more per egg but you sell less. I'd also sit Tom down and talk about whether we go down to two sheds and he gets a job somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. That's the first time today I've felt properly worried. It's like bird flu, but it doesn't go away in spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wouldn't you trust a robot with the birds?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because hens panic. One loud noise in a shed and they pile up in a corner and smother each other, I've lost two hundred birds that way in one night. Somebody has to walk in quiet and calm, and I don't believe a machine does quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it worked well on other farms, would you change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe after a few years. Tom would want one before me. I'd be the last one on the road to get one, and I know that's not clever, but it's how I am.

S4.say: That's a step too far; they should go slower and look after people. I'd say it at the farmers' meeting, which is more than I usually say.
S4.think: Big egg farms with robots would make eggs cheaper than I ever could. I wouldn't trust a robot with live birds, so I'd be the one left behind.
S4.do: Asks the packer whether they'd keep buying from small free-range farms, and if not, plans farm-gate and village-shop sales. Talks with Tom about cutting to two sheds and him finding a job elsewhere.
S4.feel: Alarmed for the first time, like bird flu that doesn't go away in spring.
S4.quote: It's like bird flu, but it doesn't go away in spring.
S4.fieldNote: She had been flat and dry until this point, and her worry arrived all at once. She compared it to bird flu, her deepest fear, which says a lot. She knows that refusing robots might leave her behind and accepts that about herself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robot one. What would help is if the packers had to keep buying a share from small farms, some kind of rule. And someone at the end of a phone who knows hens, not a website.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No. Well, maybe ask about the hens. Everyone talks about jobs, nobody asks what happens to the animals when it's all machines.

headlineQuote: Somebody has to walk in quiet and calm, and I don't believe a machine does quiet.
portrait: Uma is a 43-year-old egg farmer with twelve thousand free-range hens at Brook End, married to Tom, who keeps a few beef calves and handles anything on the computer. She has never used AI, keeps her flock records in a notebook and sits firmly in the middle politically, blaming both sides. Through the first four scenarios she is dry and mostly calm, worrying about her daughter's first job and losing the egg driver she's known for nine years. The robot scenario is the first that truly alarms her, because she won't trust a machine with live birds and knows that could leave her behind.
biggestWorry: The fast robots scenario, because big egg farms with robots would undercut her and she wouldn't trust one with live birds.
whatWouldHelp: A rule that packers keep buying a share from small farms, and a real person who knows hens at the end of a phone.
